target: AG1’s overall pro-AI case, which claims AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, work, accessibility, and safety.
objection: AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses, weakens critical thinking, repeats and exacerbates racism, and poses dangerous privacy risks; these harms are said to outweigh any conveniences or assistance AI provides.

target: AG2’s claim that AI predictably produces discriminatory outcomes and dangerous privacy harms that make it bad for society.
objection: AI deployments can include bias auditing, mitigation, access controls, and privacy-preserving methods that substantially reduce discrimination and privacy harms, so those risks are not decisive by themselves.

target: AG1’s assumption that bias auditing and other safeguards can substantially eliminate discrimination at scale.
objection: Because AI learns from real-world data and optimization processes that already reflect social disparities, discriminatory outcomes are an expected byproduct of many deployments; mitigation can reduce some harms but cannot eliminate discrimination across all relevant contexts and populations at scale.

target: AG1’s assumption that privacy protections such as access controls, differential privacy, and redaction can remove the privacy problem at scale.
objection: AI systems can still infer sensitive information from large-scale data, and privacy-preserving techniques reduce risk but do not guarantee zero leakage in all deployment settings and use cases, so privacy harm can persist even after mitigation.

target: AG2’s claim that AI weakens critical thinking skills for students and adults.
objection: AI can provide tutoring, step-by-step explanations, and tailored feedback that help learners analyze information, evaluate reasoning, and choose next steps, thereby strengthening critical thinking skills.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms economic well-being.
objection: AI can improve workplace safety, reduce losses, raise productivity, and improve health-related outcomes, all of which can increase the economic well-being of workers, students, and businesses.

target: AG2’s claim that AI harms economic well-being by itself making society worse.
objection: AI can improve health-related decisions and services, and better health increases people’s ability to work, reduces suffering, and improves daily functioning, so AI can increase economic well-being through health improvements.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is not good for society because it harms jobs and economic well-being.
objection: AI can support learning and professional workflows, improve productivity and outcomes, and thereby improve people’s economic prospects, which counters the claim of overall economic harm.

target: AG2’s privacy argument that AI inherently enables large-scale profiling from personal data and thus persistently compromises privacy.
objection: Many beneficial AI uses can be deployed with data minimization, non-personal or aggregated training data, and local or limited-retention processing, so AI need not predictably enable the kind of persistent cross-context profiling the attack assumes.

target: AG1’s data-minimization response to the privacy objection.
objection: Even data-minimized AI personalization usually still collects interaction traces and contextual signals, which can be linked over time and across contexts to infer preferences or behavior; therefore, privacy loss can persist and become re-identifiable despite reduced data collection.

target: AG2’s claim that AI personalization inevitably causes persistent cross-context privacy harm.
objection: AI services can be designed with privacy-preserving methods such as unlinkable or ephemeral identifiers, aggregation, and privacy-preserving computation that prevent persistent cross-context re-identification/profiling even when personalization uses interaction signals.

At scale, personalization requires linking a user’s past and present interactions, and users’ behavior can act as a fingerprint across services; therefore, designs relying on unlinkable identifiers and aggregation cannot reliably prevent cross-context re-identification while still supporting personalization at common scale.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy-preserving designs cannot be made to work in practice, and that AI therefore predictably undermines autonomy.
objection: AI personalization systems can give users transparency, granular consent, opt-outs, and access/delete rights, leaving people with meaningful control over data uses and preventing the kind of persistent privacy loss that would undermine autonomy in the way claimed.

target: AG1’s claim that notices, consent, opt-outs, and deletion rights are effective practical safeguards for AI personalization.
objection: In real-world systems, users often face hard-to-manage consent flows, default tracking, and reuse of data across services or third parties, making these user-control mechanisms often unavailable or ineffective in practice.
